covariance-matrix.t: The symmetric covariance matrix **S**. The dashed circle holds **unit directions**; the pink outline is the shape S turns that circle into. A long, thin shape means very unequal spread.

candidate-directions.t: For most directions **v** (blue), the transformed vector **S v** (pink) points somewhere else. The matrix both stretches and **turns** them.

eigenvector-one.t: For one special direction, **S v₁ stays on the same line as v₁**: the pink arrow lies along the yellow one. Such a direction is an **eigenvector** of S.

eigenvalue-one.t: The pink arrow is **6.03 times as long** as the yellow one, so **S v₁ = 6.03 v₁**. That stretch factor, the **eigenvalue**, is also the variance along v₁.

eigenvector-two.t: A second special direction, **perpendicular** to the first, is also kept on its own line: S v₂ is parallel to v₂.

eigenvalue-two.t: Here the stretch is only **0.17**: **S v₂ = 0.17 v₂**. A much smaller eigenvalue means much less variance along this direction.

sort-eigenvalues.t: Sort the eigenvalues from largest to smallest (**6.03, then 0.17**) and keep each eigenvector with its eigenvalue. That order ranks the directions by variance.

pc1.t: The eigenvector with the **largest eigenvalue** is the first principal component. It carries **97.2%** of the total variance.

pc2.t: The eigenvector with the next eigenvalue is PC2. It carries the remaining **2.8%** of the variance.

eigen-interpretation.t: An **eigenvector is a direction** and its **eigenvalue is the variance along it**. The dashed line shows that **−v₁ is the same axis** as v₁, so the sign of an eigenvector is arbitrary.
